text: After three lessons on metrics, logs, and traces, the obvious temptation is to wrap every function, log every branch, and emit a metric for every counter you can imagine. Don't. A system instrumented indiscriminately trades not enough data for too much data to search, and it costs real money — every series, every line, every span gets stored and usually billed by volume. This lesson is the discipline that prevents that.

Three questions cut the decision down to something tractable. Is this on a business-critical path — checkout, auth, payment — which deserves the full treatment, unlike an internal admin tool three people use? Has this broken before, or is it structurally likely to, which earns instrumentation shaped around exactly how it failed last time? And would a human actually act on this signal — if nothing would change based on seeing the value, it's noise, no matter how easy it was to add.

Here's that second question applied for real: a Redis cache caused an incident last quarter through connection pool exhaustion. So you instrument cache_pool_active_connections and cache_pool_wait_time_ms as metrics, plus an explicit log event when the pool exhausts. That's targeted instrumentation — you're not guessing what might go wrong, you're closing a gap you've already seen happen.

High-cardinality labels are a specific, expensive trap worth naming directly. Attaching a raw user ID as a metric label, instead of keeping it in logs or traces, can silently explode one metric into millions of unique time series, because every distinct label value creates a new series. Keep metrics low-cardinality — status code, route — and let logs and traces carry the high-cardinality detail instead.

Beyond the direct bill, over-instrumentation costs you alert fatigue and signal dilution. A dashboard with 200 panels, most flat lines nobody's looked at in months, is worse than fifteen that actually move when something's wrong. A service logging at DEBUG on every request in production buries the one ERROR line that mattered inside a flood nobody will read.

Treat instrumentation like code you maintain: review it, delete metrics nobody queries, prune log lines nobody searches, retire spans around removed code paths. That discipline is also where this course is headed next — observability cost is a FinOps line item, and Chapter 2 starts turning these three pillars into dashboards and alerts someone actually acts on.
